entry: Sector comprising the design, development, [[Manufacturing|manufacturing]], marketing, selling, repair and modification of motor vehicles. It is one of the world’s largest industries by revenue, with the global automotive market at about $2.75 trillion in 2025. For decades the United States led world automobile production, and its “Big Three” companies, [[General Motors]], Ford and [[Chrysler]], were for a time the world’s three largest auto manufacturers. Japan overtook the United States in 1980, and China took the top spot in 2009 with 13.8 million units; in 2024 it produced more than 31 million vehicles. Robotic equipment was introduced in the 1960s, and most cars are now mainly assembled by automated machinery. Since the 2020s, European manufacturers, including [[Volkswagen|Volkswagen Group]], have faced competition from Chinese brands, particularly in electric vehicles. ISO 26262 is considered one of the best-practice frameworks for automotive functional safety.

Autonomous region of [[Papua New Guinea]] (pop., 2024: 367,093), comprising [[Bougainville Island|Bougainville]] and Buka islands in the northern Solomon Islands archipelago. Humans have inhabited the islands for at least 29,000 years, and the region was administered at various times by Germany, Australia and Japan. The [[Civil war|Bougainville Civil War]] (1988–1998), triggered by conflict over the Panguna mine, killed up to 20,000 people. A 2019 non-binding referendum returned 98% support for independence, which requires ratification by Papua New Guinea; the target date was revised to 1 September 2030.

First-level administrative divisions of [[Spain]], created under the 1978 Constitution to guarantee limited autonomy to the nationalities and regions of Spain. There are 17 autonomous communities and two autonomous cities, [[Ceuta]] and Melilla. Each community governs itself under a Statute of Autonomy, and devolved powers vary, with regions that have stronger local nationalism typically holding more. All communities have unicameral legislatures. Foreign political scientists often describe the system as “a federal system with certain peculiarities,” while the Constitutional Court calls it the “State of Autonomous Communities.”

Medical examination of a corpse by [[Dissection|dissection]] to determine the cause, mode and manner of death, or to evaluate disease or injury. Autopsies are usually performed by a [[Pathology|pathologist]]. Only a small portion of deaths require one, as a medical examiner or coroner can usually determine the cause. Forensic autopsies establish cause and manner of death and may help identify the deceased, clinical autopsies investigate disease and confirm diagnoses made before death, and academic autopsies serve anatomical study. The term necropsy is generally used for non-human animals. Autopsies are usually carried out in cases of sudden or unnatural death, under legal authority and without the consent of relatives. [[Judaism]] and [[Islam]] usually discourage them. In most Western countries the number performed in hospitals has declined every year since 1955. A systematic review found a major diagnostic error in about 25% of autopsies, a rate that has decreased over time.

One of the four temperate [[Season|seasons]] on [[Earth]], known as fall in North American English. Outside the tropics, autumn marks the transition from summer to winter, beginning in September in the Northern Hemisphere and in March in the Southern Hemisphere. Day length decreases and temperatures cool until the [[Winter solstice]] in December (Northern Hemisphere) and June (Southern Hemisphere). In temperate climates its main feature is the change in color of deciduous trees’ leaves as they prepare to shed. Definitions vary: meteorologists use calendar months, September to November in the Northern Hemisphere, while traditional English-speaking usage ran from Lammas Day to around [[Halloween]]. Before the 16th century, *harvest* was the usual term for the season. The word autumn derives from Latin *autumnus*, possibly from an Etruscan root, and fall has origins in old Germanic languages.

American actress of Hollywood’s Golden Age, known for films including *The Killers* and *Mogambo*. She signed with [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer|MGM]] in 1941 and drew critical attention in *The Killers* (1946). In the 1950s she became a leading lady, and her performance in *Mogambo* (1953) earned an Academy Award nomination for Best Actress. She later starred opposite [[Gregory Peck]] in *On the Beach* (1959), and remained a lifelong friend of Peck. Her later films include *The Night of the Iguana*, for which she received a BAFTA Award nomination for Best Actress.

Rapid flow of [[Snow|snow]] down a slope, such as a hill or mountain. Avalanches may be triggered spontaneously by increased precipitation or weakening of the snowpack, or by people, animals or [[Earthquake|earthquakes]]. Large avalanches can capture and move ice, rocks and [[Tree|trees]]. Slab avalanches, in which tightly packed snow breaks along a weak layer, are the most hazardous type, while loose-snow avalanches start at a point and gather more snow as they descend. Fast-moving avalanches can mix with air to form powder snow avalanches. Asphyxia from burial causes most fatalities, followed by trauma and [[Hypothermia]]. Mitigation relies on snowpack assessment, forecasting and equipment such as transceivers, probes and shovels, which have improved survival rates when used effectively. Contrary to popular belief, loud sound does not trigger avalanches.

[[Buddhism|Buddhist]] bodhisattva associated with Great Compassion. Known as Lokeśvara (“Lord of the World”) in [[Sanskrit]] and as Chenrezig in Tibetan, the figure has many manifestations, including 108 forms. In some schools of [[Mahayana]] and [[Vajrayana]] Buddhism, Avalokiteśvara is considered a manifestation of Amitabha Buddha. In East Asia the bodhisattva is known as Guanyin, and a female form, White-Robed Avalokiteśvara, is widely worshiped in East Asian religions, including [[Taoism]] and Chinese folk religion. The mantra *Oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ* is the most popular in Tibetan Buddhism. Early Chinese translations, such as those by [[Xuanzang]], rendered the name as Guānzìzài.

Term for experimental or innovative [[Art|art]] and [[Literature|literature], and for the artists who create them. The word comes from the French for “advance guard” or “vanguard.” In 19th-century France the term also described reformists who sought radical political change. By the mid-19th century, avant-garde art used aesthetic innovation as a means of political and social change. Such works typically challenge established forms and are initially rejected by the artistic establishment, as with [[Dada]] (1915–1920s) and [[Surrealism]]. In 1974 Peter Bürger argued that institutions neutralize the political content of avant-garde works, while Renato Poggioli’s 1962 analysis linked avant-garde artists to bohemians. [[Marcel Duchamp]]’s readymades questioned the essence of art itself.

Epic science fiction film by [[James Cameron]], released in 2009. Set in the mid-22nd century, it follows human miners seeking the mineral unobtanium on the moon Pandora and their conflict with the indigenous Na’vi. It was the first film to gross more than $2 billion, and it won three of nine nominations at the [[Academy Awards]]. Its success increased the popularity of 3D films. Sequels *Avatar: The Way of Water* (2022) and *Avatar: Fire and Ash* (2025) followed.

Concept in [[Hinduism]] of a deity’s [[Incarnation|incarnation]] on Earth, including in human form. The term is a [[Sanskrit]] word meaning “descent.” It is most often associated with [[Vishnu]], whose avatars are central to [[Vaishnavism]]; lists include the ten [[Dashavatara]] of the Garuda Purana and twenty-two in the Bhagavata Purana. Avatars of the goddess Devi, such as [[Durga]] and [[Kali]], are common in the goddess-based [[Shaktism]] tradition. The doctrine is absent from [[Shaivism]]. Similar incarnation concepts appear in [[Buddhism]] and [[Christianity]].

American animated fantasy television series created by Michael Dante DiMartino and Bryan Konietzko. Produced by [[Nickelodeon]] Animation Studios, it aired on Nickelodeon from February 2005 to July 2008. In a world where some people can bend one of four elements, twelve-year-old Aang, the last Air Nomad and the Avatar, tries to end the Fire Nation’s war. Its style blends [[Anime|Japanese anime]] influences with American cartoons. The series won five Annie Awards and a Peabody Award, and it addresses themes rare in youth entertainment, including [[War|war]], [[Genocide]], [[Sexism]] and [[Totalitarianism]]. A [[Netflix]] live-action adaptation later followed.

Number taken as representative of a list of numbers. The arithmetic mean, the most common average, is the sum divided by the count; the average of 2, 3, 4, 7 and 9 is 5. The [[Median]], the middle value after sorting, is often used for skewed data or data with outliers, such as personal income. The harmonic mean, the reciprocal of the mean of reciprocals, suits rates such as average speed over equal distances. The [[Mode (statistics)|mode]] is the most common value and can be used for categorical data. The mean of a sample is called the sample mean, distinguished from the group mean, or [[Expected value|expected value]], of the underlying distribution. Averages are measures of central tendency.

Andalusian Muslim [[Polymath|polymath]] and jurist, known in the Western world as “The Commentator.” He served as a judge and as personal physician to a caliph. He wrote more than 100 books and treatises, including numerous commentaries on [[Aristotle]], and argued that philosophy was permissible in Islam and even compulsory for some elites. He defended philosophy against the criticism of [[Al-Ghazali]] and argued that scripture should be read allegorically where it contradicted reason. In medicine he described the signs of [[Parkinson's disease]] for the first time and proposed a new theory of [[Stroke]]. His medical book *Al-Kulliyat fi al-Tibb*, known in Latin as the *Colliget*, became a textbook in Europe for centuries. His Aristotle commentaries reignited Western interest in Greek thought, and the controversial movement called Averroism followed; the [[Catholic Church]] condemned his works in 1270 and 1277.

[[Zoroastrianism|Zoroastrian]] corpus of sacred texts, composed in the Avestan language. The texts were originally oral compositions, possibly composed between the 15th century BCE and the 4th century BCE. Written transmission began in the [[Sasanian Empire|Sasanian era]] (224–651 CE), when the Avestan alphabet was created. A multi-volume Sasanian edition was lost after the Islamic conquest of Iran, and only a portion survives, the oldest manuscript fragment dating to 1323 CE. The surviving texts include the Yasna, Visperad and Vendidad, recited by priests in ritual ceremonies, and the devotional Khordeh Avesta. The Yasna contains the Gathas, 17 hymns ascribed to [[Zoroaster]]. The texts express belief in the supreme deity [[Ahura Mazda]]. According to Zoroastrian tradition, a final revision was made under [[Khosrow I]] in the 6th century CE.

Activities and industry surrounding mechanical [[Flight|flight]], including fixed-wing and rotary-wing [[Aircraft]] and lighter-than-air craft. Aviation began in the 18th century with the [[Hot air balloon|hot air balloon]]. The first untethered human lighter-than-air flight, in a balloon designed by the [[Montgolfier brothers]], took place in 1783. Rigid [[Airship|airships]] built by the German [[Zeppelin]] company were the first aircraft to carry passengers and cargo over long distances, until the Hindenburg fire in 1937 ended the passenger era. Clément Ader made an uncontrolled, powered hop in 1890, and the [[Wright Flyer]] of the [[Wright brothers]] was the first powered airplane in the early 1900s. The introduction of the jet engine made aviation a major form of transport, and the ICAO reported 9.5 billion passengers worldwide in 2024.

Swedish DJ, remixer and record producer, born Tim Bergling. His pop-oriented house music, often blended with folk and country, helped lead [[Electronic dance music|electronic dance music]] into the mainstream. His debut album, *True* (2013), reached the top 10 in more than 15 countries, and its lead single, “Wake Me Up,” became a most-streamed song on [[Spotify]]. [[Anxiety]], [[Depression (mood)|depression]] and [[Opioid|opioid]] addiction, along with pancreatitis caused by alcohol, led him to announce his retirement from touring in 2016. He died by suicide in [[Muscat]], [[Oman]].

Evergreen tree in the laurel family, *Persea americana*, native to the [[Americas|Americas]] from Mexico to Peru. Its fruit is botanically a large [[Berry (botany)|berry]] with a single large seed, and the flesh is high in monounsaturated fats, fiber, [[Potassium]] and vitamins C, E and K. Commercial varieties have a hybrid origin, and trees are often propagated by grafting to maintain consistent fruit output. Avocados are cultivated in tropical and [[Mediterranean climate|Mediterranean]] climates. In 2024 Mexico was the world’s leading producer, supplying 25% of the global harvest of 11.2 million [[Tonne|tonnes]]. Water demand on farms strains local resources in Mexico and [[California]], and production is linked to deforestation and to partial control by organized crime in Mexico. Global warming is expected to alter suitable growing zones.

Conversion constant between an [[Amount of substance|amount of substance]] and the number of particles it contains. It is an SI defining constant with the exact value 6.02214076×10²³ mol⁻¹. The constant is named after the Italian physicist and chemist [[Amedeo Avogadro]]. It converts the average mass of one particle to its molar mass, and it relates molar volume to particle volume: for [[Water|water]], about 18 mL per mole corresponds to about 0.030 nm³ per molecule. Before the 2019 revision of the SI, it was derived from the number of atoms in 12 grams of carbon-12, and the numerical value in mol⁻¹ is called the Avogadro number.

[[Personality disorder]] characterized by marked social inhibition and avoidance, feelings of inadequacy, and strong sensitivity to rejection or negative evaluation. Also called anxious personality disorder, it leads people to avoid social interaction while strongly desiring involvement with others. Those affected often view themselves as inferior and may avoid friendships, group activities or promotions to escape criticism. Causes involve environmental and genetic factors that are not precisely known. The disorder is chronic. [[Psychotherapy]] is the primary approach, though research on treatment is limited. It affects women and men at similar rates, with some indication of higher prevalence among women.

Canadian singer and songwriter credited with boosting the popularity of female-driven pop-punk in the early 2000s. Her debut album, *Let Go* (2002), is the best-selling album of the 21st century by a Canadian artist. Its singles “Complicated” and “Sk8er Boi” earned her the title “Pop-Punk Queen.” Her second album, *Under My Skin* (2004), was her first to top the *Billboard* 200 in the United States. Her accolades include ten Juno Awards and eight [[Grammy Awards|Grammy]] nominations.

Tool with a sharpened blade attached to a handle, used to shape, split and cut wood and as a weapon. Stone hand axes without handles date from about 1.5 million years BP, and hafted axes from at least 46,000 years BP. The axe is a simple machine, a type of [[Wedge]] or dual inclined plane, and its handle acts as a [[Lever]]. Cutting axes have a shallow wedge angle for felling, while splitting axes have a more obtuse angle. Most modern axes have [[Steel|steel]] heads and wooden handles. Ground-edge stone axes were present in Japan around 38,000 years BP, and Neolithic “axe factories” in Europe produced thousands of ground stone axes, an indication of prehistoric [[Trade|trade]]. Axes of [[Copper|copper]], [[Bronze]] and [[Iron]] followed as metallurgy developed.

Angle between an object’s rotational axis and the line perpendicular to its orbital plane, also called obliquity. It causes the [[Season|seasons]] on [[Earth]], as one pole points more toward the [[Sun]] on one side of the orbit. Earth’s axial tilt is about 23.44°, decreasing at about 46.8″ per century. [[Ulugh Beg]] determined it as 23°30′17″ in 1437. [[Mars]] has a tilt of 25.2 degrees, while [[Uranus]] has an extreme obliquity of 98 degrees, so each pole alternately faces continuous sunlight or darkness for about 42 years. Under the IAU right-hand rule, [[Venus]] is tilted 177°.

Statement accepted as true to serve as a premise for further reasoning. The word comes from the Greek *axíōma*, meaning “that which is thought worthy or fit.” In classical philosophy an axiom is self-evident, while in modern logic it is simply a starting point. A non-logical axiom in mathematics makes a substantive assertion about a domain, such as a + 0 = a in [[Integer|integer]] arithmetic, and is also called a postulate or assumption. The ancient Greeks developed the logico-deductive method, in which all other assertions, called [[Theorem|theorems]], must be proved from axioms. Axiomatizing a system means deriving its claims from a small set of axioms, and there are typically many ways to do so. Whether an axiom can be called “true” is debated in the [[Philosophy of mathematics|philosophy of mathematics]].

Axiom of [[Set theory|set theory]] stating that one element can be chosen from each set in any collection of nonempty sets. Formulated in 1904 by Ernst Zermelo to formalize his proof of the well-ordering theorem, it establishes the existence of such a choice rather than constructing it. No axiom is needed when a canonical rule exists, as with the smallest number in each set of natural numbers, but it is needed for nonempty subsets of the [[Real number|real numbers]], where no such rule is known. [[Bertrand Russell]] illustrated the difference with shoes, which can be told apart as left and right, and socks, which cannot. Although initially controversial, the axiom is used by most mathematicians and is part of [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]] with the axiom of choice (ZFC). Many results, such as Tychonoff’s theorem, depend on it.
